segments.line: It's your sleeve. You
leaned on the stove while you made toast, and your sleeve has been on fire for about a minute. You
didn't feel a thing. That's the problem with invincible.
Pain isn't your body being mean. It's an alarm. And there are
real people who are born without it. Doctors call it congenital insensitivity to pain.
Kids who have it bite their tongues, walk on broken bones and
burn themselves without knowing, because nothing tells them to stop. Your
body can't be hurt. But everything you wear, hold or lean on still can. Then there's the
money. You take one stack to the bank to open an account. The
teller holds a bill up to the light. Then another. Then she lays them
side by side. Her smile doesn't move. But her other
hand slides under the desk. Every dollar bill has its own
serial number. Yours all have the same one. Every
bag the cheat gives you is the same bag, copied. So legally, you didn't get rich. You made
counterfeit money. A quarter of a million dollars of it. Forty times. The
cars are worse. They have to come from somewhere.
Einstein showed that mass and energy are the same thing.
To make one car out of nothing, about fifteen hundred kilos, you'd
need around a hundred and thirty-five billion billion joules. That's about a
fifth of all the energy the whole world uses in a year. And
every time you press that code, every light on your street flickers. And the
jetpack. Real jetpacks exist. The best ones fly for about ten minutes before the fuel runs out.
Yours never runs out.
Which is how, on Thursday afternoon, you end up three thousand feet up, in your socks, next to a plane.
